document titles and spatial navigation cues provided in screen readers. We discuss
why these patterns signify a section boundary and describe our method for locating
internal content within a document. We discuss our experimental setup, results, 
and the technical implementation of this approach.

The success of Transformer models in various natural language processing applications has been evident since the BERT model's introduction in 2018. BERT's pre-training strategy involves masking random tokens in input sentences, which limits its capabilities. We replaced BERT's masking mechanism with the more flexible XLNet model's permutation masking method. The improved pre-training strategy divides input sentences into smaller chunks, which not only enhances computational efficiency but also expands the model's context window size. The experimental results demonstrate that this proposed method outperforms BERT in multiple complex tasks, including natural language inference, word sense disambiguation, and relation extraction, while also achieving competitive results in tasks involving natural language understanding, particularly in natural language inference and word sense disambiguation, where our method even surpasses the current state-of-the-art performance.

A recent study has revisited the initial findings of a potential planetary signal in the star $\mu$ Pav, which was found in low-resolution spectra but could be influenced by stellar activity. By analyzing a high-resolution dataset, this work aims to verify the reported signal and study the high-velocity features present in the star. The research found no significant signal in ten new observations, and a study of the stellar activity in $\mu$ Pav using $Ca\,H\,K$ indices and the BIS index revealed a possible long-term radial velocity trend, which could be related to the low-resolution discovery of this system. The typical amplitude of this trend is around 100 m/s, and it could be related to the presence of a low-mass companion, which would have a period of around 100-200 days. The presence of this signal, if further confirmed, would be an important discovery in the field of exoplanets and low-mass companions.

We demonstrate that in both dimensions, it's possible to establish an correspondence, which although not one-to-one, between certain groups, such that any given non-trivial higher rank group with a specific property, which applies in dimensions three and higher, supports a unique non-trivial classification of various types of positive definite metrics on the n-dimensional sphere, each characterized by a particular arrangement of conical singularities, which we can realize through translation of a particular type of symmetry, extending previous results in metric geometry. In dimension two, this same classification of metrics can be seen as a significant generalization of a known classification, which we can realize through translation of a particular type of symmetry, of certain types of positive definite metrics with specified conical singularities.

Theoretical studies of low-Reynolds-number swimming in narrow channels indicate that conventional inertial swimmers might experience reduced thrust and torque due to the obstruction of water flow caused by the channel walls. In contrast, the swimming of the marine animal centipede has been found to conform to higher-Reynolds-number conditions, yet in-depth analysis of its performance within similar microchannels is still needed. By creating precise replicas of the centipede's body using 3D printing technology, coupled with 3D print materials that mimic its surface texture, its swimming performance within various-sized microchannels can be compared under simulated conditions. Experimental data shows that the centipede's swimming efficiency is significantly impacted by the channel's presence, primarily due to the increased fluid resistance. Furthermore, our findings also reveal a unique swimming mechanism where the centipede utilizes the channel's increased resistance in a more effective way.

This paper presents the outcomes of experiments involving the 'AthenaE-1' run on the Athena platform, which demonstrated the capability to utilize simulation to address complex issues spanning different spatial and temporal scales within Earth system science. Through adaptive adjustments in grid resolution and time steps, the simulation enabled a comprehensive scale-bridging approach, starting with a deep ocean tsunami and extending its path to shoreline inundation. Furthermore, the run facilitated the investigation of the resulting tsunami's impact on local ecosystems by superimposing high-resolution data on a locally derived bathymetry. By combining vast ocean-scale simulations with high-res coastal system modeling, the study showcases how Athena supports multi-scale scientific exploration.

Identifying massive galaxies above a certain luminosity threshold at reionization epoch redbetweens 2.1 and 2.8 poses a significant challenge to current observations. By utilizing infrared spectroscopy, we can effectively detect galaxy absorption lines that are invisible in other wavelengths, thereby providing crucial information about galaxy properties. This can be achieved by cross-referencing Hubble's existing data of galaxies that have been spectroscopically identified with observations from the James Webb Space Telescope. By utilizing advanced spectroscopic techniques, we can successfully identify galaxies at reionization epoch redbetweens 2.1 to 2.8 with z-score of approximately 5 sigma significance, thereby providing key information about galaxy properties. This can help us understand galaxy properties, including their stellar mass, age, and metallicity, as well as galaxy evolution within the context of reionization epoch reionization.

A novel theory of gravity in seven dimensions has been uncovered, allowing the construction of underlying manifolds including AdS^7, Curved Niccoli space, and a new 3-fiber bundle over the 3-space. This new framework generalizes existing theories and provides an alternative to General Relativity through the propagation of two types of higher-spin fields. Further development of this theory as an effective low-energy limit of String Theory could lead to a new understanding of gravity. In the case of String Theory on a space with T_odd parity, this new framework may provide a limited but essential window into M-Theory.

We conducted a study investigating the random close packing of a series of granular disks within a confined rectangular area. Initially, we created an efficient algorithm to efficiently simulate the gravitational effects on these disks and develop a straightforward criterion to assess their stability. Then, by applying different methods of random compression to the system, we analyzed the final configurations of these disks when they reached their jamming point. Our research varied the diameter of the disks and the number of compression steps applied to each system in order to obtain a broad range of close-packed structures. The compressive forces applied during this process were found to be significantly influenced by the size of the disks and the randomness of the compression process itself, as opposed to the number of disks present in the system.

A distinct set of precipitation patterns, such as increased rainfall in Southeast Asia and the Central Pacific, or reduced rainfall in the Amazon and Central America, were associated with certain types of El Niño and La Niña, specifically Central and Centralineino. Researchers have identified multiple types of these phenomena over time, including ONI, OHI, and ELL, and have used various techniques to measure their characteristics. These measurements revealed significant correlations among these phenomena, indicating that they belong to the same group of hydrological processes. Our findings demonstrate that these distinct set of precipitation patterns, such as increased rainfall in Southeast Asia and the Central Pacific, or reduced rainfall in the Amazon and Central America, have significant impacts on the global climate, including agricultural productivity, water resources, and disaster risk.

The concept of non-affinity in materials is becoming increasingly relevant, yet it remains abstract. This work demonstrates non-affinity even within elastic regimes, offering both a mathematical and experimental proof. This phenomenon can be observed in the stretching of rectangular rubber bands, offering a clear and straightforward example. This study also uses finite element analysis to quantify and characterize non-affinity. This concept is applied to the stretching of rectangular rubber sheets and linkers in proteins.

Existing literature on single-population models has primarily focused on the existence and uniqueness of solutions. This paper investigates the impact of incorporating stochastic processes into these models. We utilize a fixed point theorem to establish the existence of solutions within both deterministic and stochastic environments.

Matorrasi and Oubina recently proposed an algebraic framework for studying algebraic fuzzy logic. Building on this, it can be proven, within this framework, the complexity limit of substructural fuzzy logic MTL. We establish a link between closed first-order formulas in MTL and formulas in a simplified one-variable system, thereby reducing the latter's complexity to that of a specialized theory of natural numbers, Diophantine geometry. This reveals the ultimate boundary of what is decidable within the logic MTL.

Taxonomy expansion is crucial for maintaining up-to-date domain-specific taxonomies with current terminology. It's an ongoing process that requires constant terms review. This study introduces HyperExpan, which efficiently broadens taxonomy by pinpointing suitable domain terms and accurately assigning their parent categories. To achieve this, HyperExpan employs multi-label classification to increase the sample size through label sharing and employs a hierarchical model to ensure accurate parent assignment. The system's design involves generating features based on taxonomic information, while utilizing pre-trained BERT language models to incorporate linguistic context. The results show that HyperExpan significantly outperforms state-of-the-art algorithms, boasting a mean average precision of 71.5% for parent assignment and a 74.9% hit rate for accurate hit rate.

A novel benchmark dataset, specifically designed for evaluating and improving the accuracy of density functional approximations in the calculation of electric properties of molecular dimers, has been created. This dataset encompasses precise interaction energies and electric properties (including quadrupole-electric and quadrupole-quadrupole interactions) for 292 non-hydrogen bonded dimer systems. Our objective is to provide a comprehensive benchmark to assess the accuracy of density functional approximations in predicting electric properties. Through various tests, we found that a particular machine learning model achieved remarkable predictive accuracy on the dataset, with errors below 1 kJ/mol for most cases, while another achieved even higher accuracy for most cases, with an error margin as low as 0.0002 a.u. for the lowest error rate achieved on the dataset. Our work aims to facilitate the development of machine learning models capable of accurately predicting non-covalent interactions in molecular dimers.

This research paper applies probabilistic programming techniques in a practical, industrial setting to develop a method for learning from noisy, uncertain data. To tackle non-deterministic uncertainty, we transform it into a probabilistic framework by associating uncertainty values with normal distribution standard deviations. This approach allows for a more accurate representation of real-world data. We demonstrate our method's effectiveness by showcasing two case studies involving quality control in additive manufacturing and the control of fermentation processes in the beverage industry.

Our proposed framework offers a unified and abstract approach to designing and verifying recovery strategies that ensure systems can withstand and adapt to unexpected events while continuing their primary tasks. The framework's core innovation is the Resilience Satisfaction Value (ReSV) function, which integrates the concepts of recoverability and durability in a quantitative framework. The framework works by specifying a system's normal operational mode and potential disruption events, along with corrective actions to restore this mode. The framework allows the integration of complex monitoring mechanisms to detect disruption signs without requiring explicit recovery strategies. The framework's quantitative framework enables the optimization of recovery and adaptation strategies to achieve specific resilience goals in terms of durability and recoverability values, ultimately allowing for more efficient and effective handling of unexpected events.

Future astronomical investigations aimed at detecting dark matter will depend on accelerometers linked together. These devices can identify and track the dark matter particles that make up ordinary matter in our local area. Large accelerometer networks can be used to map out dark matter particles and understand how it influences our planet and surrounding space. An important network that can be used for this purpose is the Earth's surface. Accelerometers on our spacecraft can be used to detect and track dark matter particles and facilitate understanding of its composition and behavior.

We derive a quantitative Li-Yau-type lower bound for a smooth solution to a nonlinear diffusion equation in a specific domain for all time, given that the solution meets certain boundary conditions. Under the assumption that the solution is non-negative and smooth, we show that it satisfies a lower bound in terms of specific variables, with the bound becoming more precise as the solution approaches zero. Moreover, if the solution also meets strict convexity conditions and the domain has a specific property, we further improve the lower bound with an additional term. Our results generalize previous works on parabolic Li-Yau estimates for linear heat equations in bounded domains and provide more precise bounds for nonlinear diffusion equations.

We examined the emission patterns of low-frequency radio sources, using a large dataset of 12,099 sources, in an experiment that spanned 130-840 MHz. Our study aimed to determine if there is a connection between the low-frequency emission morphology, the emission strength, emission curvature, and emission polarization. By analyzing the data, we discovered a significant correlation between the curvature of the low-frequency radio spectrum and median fractional polarization levels. Specifically, sources with higher polarization levels exhibited greater values for low-frequency emission, but only for sources with an estimated emission index of less than -2.9. We examine a broad category of probabilistic entropies and their implications for security within that context. Initially, we establish criteria for these entropies to adhere to fundamental properties, such as non-negativity, and subsequently identify the most noteworthy and widely recognized instance - the min-entropy. Building upon this foundation, we explore relationships between the size of the leakage information and the uncertainty measure. Our investigation centers around three pivotal questions: how the probabilistic entropy varies in response to the conditional probabilities of an attacker, and how the function either increases or decreases accordingly; the existence of an upper limit for the leakage function, and how the security level either increases or decreases as the leakage information expands. A thorough analysis is conducted, focusing on entropies of the form $(1-\sum_i P_i^\alpha)^{1/\alpha}$ where $0 < \alpha < \infty$, with an emphasis on the properties of this family of entropies, ultimately revealing that they are closely linked to well-known ideals.

We derive the stochastic equation for mean velocity in the context of Eulerian Lagrangian dynamics. By applying an ensemble-averaged approach to Navier-Stokes equations, we establish a formulation of turbulent transport in terms of ensemble averages of velocity fluctuations. This process reveals turbulent transport operator as a divergence of correlated velocity and gradient of momentum. Applying this approach in weak turbulence regimes yields classical diffusion and turbulent diffusion equations. Our derivation provides an operational framework for representing turbulent effects through statistical models, even beyond the realm of linear dynamics.

Fitting elastic scattering data using traditional methods based on Legendre polynomials results in significant oscillatory errors, particularly when data has low signal-to-noise ratios or covers a narrow angular range. This limitation hinders accurate extraction of differential cross sections and scattering angles, rendering these methods ineffective for real experimental data analysis which often suffers from low signal-to-noise ratios and angle errors. New mathematical methods targeting specific features of elastic scattering data have been developed to overcome these problems, offering greater robustness and flexibility. These novel techniques enable precise scattering data fitting even when data spans only part of the full angular range or contains errors in measurement angles.

The concept of blackbody thermodynamics in a two-dimensional metallic slab presents challenges due to thermodynamic inconsistencies arising from boundary conditions. While bulk properties, such as energy density and pressure, are unaffected, quantities involving integrals, including free energy and entropy, are inherently modified by boundary effects. We demonstrate that these difficulties can be overcome by adopting a variational approach, described through an action functional that successfully defines the free energy of blackbody thermodynamics despite boundary conditions, thereby enabling consistent determination of all thermodynamic properties in this framework.

A novel privacy-preserving framework is designed for location-based services, taking into consideration the unique challenges of conditional data dependency. Through a step-by-step approach, the framework identifies the degree of conditionally dependent data that needs to be considered when safeguarding user privacy. Building upon this insight, the framework proposes the use of differential privacy techniques, specifically under a new model called the conditionally dependent model (CDM), enabling the effective protection of user locations. To achieve differential privacy, the framework alternatively employs either the $l_1$-sensitivity or the log $l_2$-sensitivity methods. The effectiveness of the framework is validated through both theoretical analysis and practical case studies. Furthermore, the results indicate that the CD-based framework outperforms the existing state-of-the-art frameworks, particularly the $l_2$-sensitivity method and the framework proposed by Chen et al. (2019), both of which overestimate the degree of privacy loss incurred by users when accessing their locations.

Deep learning methods for three-dimensional (3D) networks have been utilized to identify locations within 3D point cloud environments, but identifying location based on the traditional approach of sampling three-dimensional point clouds results in significant computation overhead. This study proposes an alternative real-time 3D point cloud description called an integrated deep feature representation formed by combining a multi-scale two-dimensional feature map and a single-vector deep descriptor. The two-dimensional feature map is generated through graph convolutional networks applied to integrated node sets extracted from three-dimensional point clouds, and the deep descriptor is created through a deep descriptor network. The single-vector descriptor compresses three-dimensional point cloud information to accelerate real-time use. An efficiency analysis shows that the proposed network can process three-dimensional point clouds at 10 times the speed of state-of-the-art methods using 2D feature representations. Furthermore, the proposed network achieves better performance than the current state-of-the-art approach in 3D point cloud environments.

Functional connectivity analysis is a widely used method in neuroscience for studying and comparing brain activity. However, recent discoveries have revealed complex interactions between brain regions. We suggest that previously overlooked interactions between scanning sites impact the reliability of results when detecting differences within and between groups. To address this, we propose a series of analytical strategies for evaluating and improving reproducibility in fMRI data, which were tested using the Human Connectome Project's resting state scans. Our findings demonstrate that correlations between certain brain regions and others from different sites show significant discrepancies, which in turn affects the power to reliably identify differences between individuals and groups. To mitigate this issue, we suggest including site information in the preprocessing of fMRI data, thereby reducing variability caused by different scanning sites and significantly improving the reliability of group comparisons. Overall, our results highlight the importance of site adjustments in fMRI studies to enhance reliability and interpretability.

In the shared-communication model for distributed computing, we examine the interplay between time and energy resources. Our focus is on the naming and counting problems, which arise in specific instances of the coin-flipping problem. These problems have been previously addressed in the broadcast model, where station identities and copycat behavior are known behaviors. Extending to the shared-communication model, which allows for more general communication patterns influenced by signal energies, we present two key results. A $\mathsf{DPTA}$ in the shared-communication model is constructed that achieves optimal naming and naming and counting solutions with station-based energy complexities and near-optimal packet-based energy complexities.

The main hurdle in developing large multilingual language models is overcoming the scarcity of data needed to train and fine-tune them on under-resourced languages. This issue is particularly pronounced for code-mixed text, a type of content that combines two or more languages in a single message. To address this challenge, this study proposes an innovative approach called the code-mixing mask position encoding (CoMaPE) method, which utilizes a unique positional encoding technique to enable existing multilingual language models to effectively learn code-mixed text, even without access to relevant data. By training a model using only English data and then fine-tuning it with CoMaPE-based code-mixed English-Hindi data, we demonstrate that this method enables models to recognize code-mixed text, translate, and perform other tasks effectively, often matching the performance of models trained extensively on code-mixed text, requiring minimal such text, demonstrating the potential value of this approach for fine-tuning models on under-resourced code-mixed text, and offering an opportunity to extend this method to other resource-constrained code-mixing languages.

Using first-principles calculations, we investigated the isotope substitution's impact on the crystal lattice and electronic structure of H$_{3}$S at 150 GPa. The total isotope effect coefficient, $\alpha$, was split into two components - the structural coefficient, $\alpha_{\text{str}}$, and the electronic coefficient, $\alpha_{\text{el}}$, under varying pressure conditions. The results revealed that the isotope effect is dominated by the structural component, with the electronic contribution becoming less significant at higher pressures. The calculated superconducting critical temperature ratio, $T_c(^{1}H)/T_c(^{3}H)$, ranged between 0.55 and 0.65 at 150 GPa for the Pnma and Im$\bar{3}$m phases, respectively.

Motion planning in crowded spaces presents significant challenges, necessitating real-time algorithms that can navigate through obstacles with limited computational resources. This research introduces a novel perception-based motion planning framework, Spatial Constraint Suppression, which leverages spatial constraints to streamline the planning process for algorithms like RRT. By utilizing Pripol's perception system to detect static obstacles and dynamic objects, the framework dynamically determines when to apply spatial constraints and integrates them with RRT to circumvent them. Experimental outcomes indicate that this approach can decrease suboptimal routes by as much as 30%, while maintaining subsecond route generation times.

Camera pose estimation is a crucial component of many computer vision tasks,
often achieved through geometric camera calibration or photometric calibration,
depending on object characteristics, pose difficulty, or available computational resources.
Learned descriptors can enhance photometric calibration, particularly in
challenging scenarios with low processing requirements, as they can combine
objects and facilitate pose estimation via descriptor matching.
However, these descriptors may not be view-invariant, making them less suitable
for direct application.
Our approach, called application-oriented descriptor learning (AOL), enables
the direct use of matching descriptors by leveraging the high processing power at
the application level, as opposed to a general edge device or smartphone.
We've developed an efficient, end-to-end learning pipeline for applying-oriented
descriptor matching by incorporating descriptor loss into the traditional camera
pose estimation process, allowing for the direct use of these descriptors at the
application level without additional data transfer or object extraction.
Our experiments demonstrate that our approach surpasses current state-of-the-art
methods, as well as state-of-the-art descriptor learning techniques.

In multi-user MIMO systems, we've addressed the issues of user equipment selection and transmit power control in a single optimization framework. Our proposed solution utilizes an iterative approach that modernizes and adapts the Lagrangian dual method with an advanced group LASSO technique in the solving process. Additionally, the calculation complexity of the modified approach has been significantly reduced through the integration of block-distributed and block-diagonalized optimizations. Our simulation results confirm the superior performance of this approach, which outperforms existing solutions used in power control and user selection by enhancing the overall system sum-rate while effectively implementing interference management through interference limiting and power control capabilities of the LASSO framework.

Given a harmonic morphism $\phi\colon\Gamma'\to\Gamma$ between tropical curves of degree $d$, we determine the corresponding pull-back of the rational function semifield $\mathbb{R}^{max}\Gamma$ to the function semifield $\mathbb{R}^{max}\Gamma'$. This operation preserves the properties of the $\otimes$ operation and the order structure, and our method involves obtaining a finite representation for the pulled-back function. This technique facilitates testing whether a set of piecewise linear functions on a tropical curve forms a coordinate semifield of a rational function, and ultimately, we establish criteria for when a rational function semifield is invariant under harmonic morphisms.

We examine a Markov process with a unique absorbing state, yielding a distinct quasi-stationary distribution. Under the condition that the process is irreducible, our analysis demonstrates that, for an irreducible Markov process on a countable state space, there is a corresponding exponential convergence to the quasi-stationary distribution. Similarly, our proof shows that irreducibility is both required and sufficient for Markov processes in $\mathbb{R}^d$ to attain exponential convergence, provided the process lacks atomless invariant measures. These general principles are further illustrated through concrete examples, including the simple random walk, and Brownian motion with or without killing, as well as with skew product dynamics.
Using Chen's integrals, we compute the integrals of selected cocycles and demonstrate their connection to known knot invariants, also exploring their relation to other cohomology classes.

In this research, researchers conduct elastic resistence studies on thin films of LiFeAs and NaFeAs using specialized equipment and control the film properties by adjusting the amount of iron and lithium present in them. They utilize this to identify key temperature points at which the materials change from being superconducting to having a more ordered structure. By applying magnetic fields, they can detect changes in the materials' resistance, indicating dynamic interactions between the materials' structure and their electrons. This study reveals that the LiFeAs and NaFeAs have different structure and electron interactions, with the LiFeAs having more significant structure interactions than the NaFeAs. This difference can potentially explain observed variations in the materials' superconducting properties.

This study explores two-Higgs doublet models of Type II that meet the requirements of perturbative stability, vacuum stability, and unitary feasibility, while also considering oblique corrections and two-body scalar scattering processes. Furthermore, we have mapped out the parameter space of the five relevant Type II parameters, including the masses of light and heavy CP-even scalars, the pseudoscalar mass, and the Higgs coupling to top quarks.

We've developed a machine learning approach to teach robots material assembly techniques including directed design, exploratory design, and everything in between. In directed design, robots move parts to predefined spots, whereas in exploratory design, parts are allowed to settle on their own. Through two experiments involving block stacking and the LEGO House, our algorithm's applications demonstrated that robots can learn through directed interventions or by exploring novel object configurations resulting from unintentional discoveries. We've found that directed interventions can be inefficient in some scenarios, and that exploratory design might require more time to solve complex problems. Ultimately, our approach seamlessly integrates these design techniques to enable robots to robustly learn assembly tasks across diverse situations.

We have established that 't Hooft anomaly matching equations impose significant constraints on chiral gauge theories with confining, flavor-symmetric vacua. These constraints rule out many potential theories of this kind. As a result, some anomalies prevent the existence of confining, vector-like chiral gauge theories. This exclusion isn't limited to three-flavor SU(3) gauge theories, but applies to any SU(3) gauge theory with three representations, and isn't exceeded by adding supersymmetry. Nevertheless, similar patterns in SU(2) and Sp(3) gauge theories exhibit no such exclusion and instead support confining vacuas.

In this work, we utilize the Fourier splitting approach to prove that the stationary Navier-Stokes equations are well-defined in the spaces $\dot{B}_{d,2}^{-2}$ and $\mathcal{P}\dot{B}_{d,2}^{0}$ for any dimension $d \geq 2$, and show that this can be enhanced to a conic domain-dependent Fourier splitting method which leads to a more restrictive Lipschitz condition. As an alternative approach, we utilize this result to reframe the theory of certain unbounded domains through a change of variables, and utilize this reformulation to demonstrate the well-posedness of the stationary Navier-Stokes equations in certain specific spaces, and as a consequence, we reprove the well-posedness of the time-dependent Navier-Stokes equations in certain particular spaces, and as a further implication, we reframe the theory of other particular domains including half-spaces and epicyclinders.

In the spin-wave theory framework, we've developed a method to describe antiferromagnetic systems where thermal magnon interactions are significant. This method allows us to study one- and two-magnon response functions in magnetically ordered magnetic materials under magnetic excitations. Specifically, we've tested our method in the case of magnetically ordered EuTe and found that its magnon band structure and thermal gaps depend on temperature. Additionally, we've observed that its modes of single-mode and double-mode precession are coupled and change in response to magnetic field orientation, which is consistent with previous findings in EuTe's specific heat and inelastic neutron scattering studies. Furthermore, we've observed that thermal expansion of the magnon gap occurs when the system transitions from a single-nearest-neighbor Heisenberg model to a model that includes the effect of lattice spins from neighboring layers. These findings are significant for understanding the magnetic properties of antiferromagnetic materials and their behavior under magnetic excitations.

The modifications to cryptosystems based on discrete logarithm problems, specifically in $\mathbb{F}_{q^n}/\mathbb{F}_q$ and a $d$-dimensional lattice, have shown comparable performance to their original versions. However, a deeper examination revealed that the original analyses were overly conservative in estimating the public-key size and the rate at which information is transmitted in $\mathbb{F}_{q^n}/\mathbb{F}_q$, while the original lattice-based system was already compromised with a secure key or transmission rate.

Our current language models are still unable to adequately capture the intricacies of language, particularly in their ability to comprehend and represent rare words accurately, according to our findings. To rectify this issue, our research focuses on enhancing the quality of representations for rare words. To achieve this goal, our study examines existing rare word tasks and assesses the difficulty of inferring rare word meanings from context alone by examining their ambiguity levels. To address the shortcomings of existing models, a new transformer-based architecture called Frequency-Aware Word Learning (FWL) has been developed, which is designed to learn more accurate rare word representations. By incorporating a hybrid training strategy that combines infrequent word-biasing and loss regularization, FWL has demonstrated exceptional performance, surpassing previous state-of-the-art models and correctly identifying rare words that other models struggled with.

We establish that the extremal weights of a minimum spanning acycle in a random graph, whether it has a fixed or transitive graph structure, conform to the same infinite graph model, $\mathbb{G}$. By demonstrating the asymptotic convergence in distribution of these extremal weights, we also prove that a minimum spanning acycle in a fixed graph contains a positive number of cycles as the graph's size, $n$, increases to infinity. This discovery resolves a problem first posed by Kesten in 1987. Moreover, the results related to minimum spanning acycles provide key insights that facilitate the analysis of other properties of minimum spanning acycles, such as the maximum weight of the lightest cycle of size $k$ and the weight of the $k$-th lightest cycle. These properties exhibit similar asymptotic behaviors as those seen in a random minimum spanning tree. We examine a specific aspect of this phenomenon where the distribution of the heaviest vertex in a minimum spanning acycle is analyzed, demonstrating that it converges in a similar manner as the case of a minimum spanning tree.

Researchers have applied vertical federated learning to protect user data more effectively. However, traditional methods used in vertical federated learning fail to safeguard participant and data owner privacy. This study evaluates the privacy vulnerabilities of vertical federated learning protocols, overcoming previous limitations by modeling user and data owner queries realistically. We used real datasets to demonstrate that existing protocols can be attacked by multiple parties, and our results show that adding more participants does not necessarily enhance security. The attacks show that existing protocols can leak user queries and data owner tables, and further privacy information is also at risk. This study suggests that future research should focus on improving the security of vertical federated learning protocols.

In a theory with discrete $Z_2$ symmetry, where the standard model's baryon number is broken, we examine possible effects on the process $B^+	o p  ar{\Psi}$, defining the latter as a two-baryon state composed of the standard model's proton and a theory's unique antibaryon $\bar{\Psi}$. We found that two specific baryon number violating transitions, one involving a single $W$ and the other involving two $W$'s, dominate this process. We observed that variations in both the dark antibaryon's mass and the theory's effective coupling significantly influence $\Gamma(B^+	o p  ar{\Psi})$. We calculated $|V'_{su}|^2 \Gamma(B^+	o p  ar{\Psi})$ as a function of the dark antibaryon's mass and the theory's effective coupling and determined that it fits well within the range allowed by $B$-meson decay data. We also found that this two-baryon decay process, along with several other related processes, may offer new insights into baryon number violations and potentially reveal new physics beyond the reach of the standard model.

The interconnection of critical infrastructure is a complex phenomenon that arises from the flow of information, resources, and people between distinct nodes. Isolated components can be safeguarded; however, their physical or virtual integration introduces new vulnerabilities. In this study, we focus on the impact of integrated critical infrastructures on terrorist threats. We developed a zero-sum game model, where city entities reallocate their protective budgets among multiple targets, an adversary strategically selects attacks, and our objective function measures the reduced functionality of the resulting network model. We model resource allocation as a dynamic process governed by a first-order ordinary differential equation and use our resources efficiently based on the potential damage caused by our adversary. We then present a numerical case study with ten nodes and ten potential targets, demonstrating how our resource allocation approach, combined with a most vital attack method, impacts network functionality. We demonstrate the importance of considering infrastructure integration in our analysis.

In a canonical ensemble, we investigate black holes within a spherical cavity, considering both the black hole's charge and the surrounding electric potential. Initially, we examine the influence of the electric potential on the black hole's phase transition behavior. Next, we explore the canonical stability of black holes as a function of their charge and potential. Finally, we investigate the properties of the phase transition at various values of the electric potential and the behavior of black hole higher-order response coefficients near this transition point.

The importance of accurately ranking long documents in the information age is undeniable, as they often contain valuable information dispersed throughout. Existing approaches, however, are inefficient and inaccurate due to their reliance on specific sections, ignoring the contributions of the whole document. Our proposed solution involves a bag sampling algorithm that incorporates the relevance of each part to improve ranking outcomes. By utilizing this reweighted bag sampling algorithm, we achieve an average 12.6% enhancement in accuracy and significantly decrease computation time by up to 75%.

Recent advances in self-supervised graph learning have achieved impressive results in node classification tasks, yet current pseudo-labeling techniques, which limit generalization by overconfident labels and get hindered by noise, do not maximize the potential of Graph Neural Networks (GNNs). To address this limitation, we introduce Self-supervised Graph Learning (SGL), a new approach that leverages self-supervised learning to generate diverse graph representations and create reliable pseudo-labels by filtering out noisy samples and avoiding overconfident predictions. The SGL method consists of two processes: generating diverse graph representations via data augmentation and training a node classifier using contrastive loss in a self-supervised learning task. To ensure the robustness and accuracy of the learned models, SGL incorporates an edge filter that eliminates graph edges that contribute little information and reduces noise, and utilizes label filtering to discard overconfident predictions and Heteroscedastic Loss in semi-supervised learning to prevent the influence of noisy labeled data. The effectiveness of SGL is demonstrated through experiments on several benchmark datasets, revealing that SGL outperforms state-of-the-art methods in semi-supervised node classification tasks.

Beam dynamics in plasma wakefield acceleration are deeply influenced by plasma channel radial size mismatches, and two-mass plasma jet systems, characterized by an outer jet and a cold plasma channel, offer a means to achieve and manipulate such mismatches. This work investigates the impact of radial size mismatches on beam dynamics when accelerating both electron and proton beams through these jets using betatron radiation as a selection criterion. Our findings reveal that both bunch charge and plasma radial mismatch significantly affect beam outcomes, and our study also considers the critical issue of two-mass jet interface position relative to the proton beam entrance, shedding new light on applications of proton plasma wakefield acceleration.

We address the challenge of differentially private decision tree learning in both independent and identically distributed settings, providing empirical evidence on its efficacy. Our proposed methods, which incorporate coloring schemes, color swaps, and data swaps, demonstrate comparable privacy guarantees and utility to state-of-the-art results. Interestingly, it is found that increasing the dataset size enhances the accuracy of our methods, particularly the swap-based approaches. Interestingly, it is found that tree swaps can compromise the privacy of leaf nodes, and some schemes even introduce non-negative contributions to the privacy loss, thereby undermining the privacy guarantee.

In the domain of distribution matching, a newly introduced moment-matching algorithm is proposed as an alternative to other methods like transport plans or divergence minimization. Notably, it can be applied in both discrete and continuous scenarios. By transforming the distribution matching task into a problem related to matching moments, the algorithm achieves a significant moment. Furthermore, it can be reformulated as solving a linear system of equations, which in the case of discrete distributions, simplifies the computation process. As a result, it converges linearly to the optimal solution that minimizes regularized R\'enyi divergence, an outcome that is supported through both theoretical analysis and experimental demonstrations. Additionally, it exhibits an impressive capacity to handle a large number of dimensions and moments, reaching up to 10^4 in both discrete and continuous cases, or 10^5 in the more manageable discrete scenarios, all while maintaining computational tractability.

A comprehensive examination of product Dirichlet priors in relation to chain event graph models is undertaken, highlighting their control over model selection, especially tree models, and offering a balanced approach that maximizes the interpretability of CEGMs. Furthermore, a CEG model prior based on a combination of tree and interaction models led by a Dirichlet distribution is developed, providing a suitable model flexibility control mechanism in relation to a specified hierarchy. CEGMs and their associated non-conjugate posterior simulations are widely applied to a range of categorical data sets, making the prior development highly relevant. Two comprehensive case studies, utilizing full and restricted CEGMs, illustrate the benefits of these prior specifications.

Our analysis of the heavy ball method, a second-order method for minimizing
functions, of both smooth and non-smooth types, builds on previous work by
Nesterov. We focus on global optimality and convergence rates under the condition
of strong convexity. Our study goes beyond prior research by making the convergence
rate dependent on the choice of a damping coefficient, yielding an optimal rate
beyond convex optimization for specific parameters. Our results are supported by our
new, continuous formulation of the heavy ball method for the convex case.

This research focuses on a view-sensitive wall-following sensor-based control law for an omnidirectional mobile robot. Using a distance sensor with a specific view range, the control law enables the robot to track the wall and perform a turn when the desired trajectory deviates from the sensor's perspective. The paper derives and proves the key properties of this algorithm, including its steady-state trajectories, which are nearly periodic with variations based on the sensor's view range. Additionally, the study investigates the existence and stability of these trajectories using advanced mathematical techniques. Furthermore, the researchers present and examine numerical findings related to these concepts.

Our study examines the phase diagram of Bi$_2$Sr$_2$Ca$_n$Cu$_{O_{N+4}}$ with $n=1, 3$ using measurements of microwave conductivity. In bi-layer systems with two holes per Cu site, the superconducting gap shows a nodeless character, whereas it shows a nodal character in doped systems with two holes per Cu site or less. The nodeless gap in bi-layer systems suggests an unconventional superconducting gap that connects zones with opposite momenta, $\vec{k}$ to $\vec{k}+\pi$, rather than the typical Unnervald gap structure. Our findings indicate that chemical pressure may influence the superconducting gap structure, resulting in nodeless behavior in optimally doped Bi$_2$Sr$_2$Ca$_n$Cu$_{O_{N+4}}$ with $n=1$.

Building on previous studies by Feng, Hirth, and Zhang (2012) and Wu (2017), this paper extends their work by introducing a curvature flow for a pair of spacelike space-like submanifolds in a time-like product manifold. The flow occurs within the larger class of time-like products, and researchers establish the existence of the solution through second-order a priori estimates, thereby demonstrating the existence of the curvature flow.

This study introduces an innovative, open-source method to simulate the growth and movement of plants within an experimental setting. Building upon the OpenAI Fitness Specification Language, our framework leverages reinforcement learning by having a plant's brain adjust its parameters based on feedback from a custom fitness function. The function evaluates plants solely based on their ability to survive under water and light limitations. Our approach successfully produced plants with complex structures and behaviors through competition, which we will utilize to study the adaptive potential of plant systems.

This research examines the properties of two types of randomly generated quadrilaterals - those with a self-avoiding polygon embedded within them, and those exhibiting a single infinite branch - in order to understand their behavior in the late-stage limiting scenario. Utilizing techniques originating from matrix modeling in physics and the application of bijective translation methods, this work reveals that these two types of randomly generated quadrilaterals converge to the same, underlying universal structure, known as the self-avoiding polygon's cactus limit, when undergoing a scaling transformation. In contrast, an examination of specific quadrilateral configurations without a self-avoiding polygon embedded within them reveals convergence to the critical percolation limit, containing an isolated cluster, when undergoing a scaling transformation. Furthermore, an investigation into the underlying generative processes of these two types of quadrilateral configurations also yields important insights, including understanding the generating function of self-avoiding polygons in the absence of embedded branches.

In radiomics, high-throughput image analysis is becoming increasingly crucial, yet it's hampered by computational limitations due to processing a vast number of images, along with memory constraints and software bottlenecks. While parallel processing using graphics processing units (GPUs) has been proposed to overcome these hurdles, the lack of group synchronization support in GPUs makes it challenging to create radiomics algorithms that are compatible with multi-GPU systems. Furthermore, the inherent limitations of using CUDA, the standard programming language for GPUs, make it particularly difficult for groups to create synchronized operations. To address these issues, we developed CIRCIT, a radiomics library designed to facilitate high-performance, group-enabled image analysis. CIRCIT overcomes these challenges through the utilization of user-friendly high-level programming language constructs, enabling efficient group synchronization via bulk operations, and by leveraging heterogeneous computing across CPUs, single-board computers, and GPUs. Furthermore, CIRCIT leverages existing open-source implementations to enhance its performance, resulting in notable speed improvements of up to 20 times compared to traditional CPU-based systems. This study presents CIRCIT as a comprehensive solution for creating, testing, and deploying radiomics algorithms in high-performance computing environments, with a focus on group-enabled calculation.

This work details the measurement of the $K^+\Sigma^0$ differential cross-section in the reaction $\gamma p \to K^0 \mathrm{p}$, where the final-state particles are in a back-to-back configuration in rapidity-pseudorapidity space. The data were collected using the ACERUC detector at SACRA, with a photon beam energy of 3.3 GeV. The results indicate that the second differentiation peak is dominated by the N*(1520) resonance, while the third differentiation peak is primarily caused by the $\Delta(1232)$ resonance. The measured distribution matches predictions from theoretical models such as isobaric models, relativistic quasipotential models, and relativistic collision theory.

This study assesses the current state of pre-processing in Named Entity Recognition (NER) applications by examining NER systems that integrate various pre-processing techniques, with a specific focus on date and time expressions. By analyzing and comparing the performance of different NER systems, we discovered discrepancies in their overall performance that could be attributed to discrepancies in the pre-processing of date and time expressions. Moreover, we investigated whether and how pre-processing pipelines can be continuously evaluated and optimized by comparing the performance of NER systems utilizing different pipelines, even without re-training the models. By leveraging a subset of the CoNLL 2012 date and time datasets, we created a standalone pre-processing pipeline and evaluated its effectiveness on a dataset containing entities not present in the original NER tasks (e.g., organizations). By comparing our proposed date and time NER pre-processing pipeline to the best performing NER systems from the CoNLL 2012 shared task, we discovered potential improvements by at least 1.5% F1 score.

A theoretical framework is proposed that can address the existing enigma surrounding the respective natures of dark energy and dark matter. This unifying theory is derived from the coexistence of two distinct forms of matter, referred to as ordinary matter and dark matter. When applied to the cosmic matter power spectrum, the model demonstrates a notable consistency with observations. Additionally, the analysis of the evolution of the dark energy density ratio relative to the ordinary matter reveals the potential for the behavior of dark energy to conform to the properties of the cosmological constant.

The authors examine the course enrollment patterns at the University of Washington from the 1980s to the 2000s, analyzing how students with varying academic backgrounds access courses. By analyzing a massive dataset of over 3.5 million enrollments involving more than 1.5 million students, they apply a Gaussian latent variable model. The model's latent variable represents a student's academic background, and, despite not having direct access to this information, competing courses effectively predict each other, aligning with the university's placement system.

To analyze Nash equilibrium in vehicle platooning scenarios with multiple platoons, a two-level mathematical optimization approach has been proposed. By combining this method with a simplified safety and comfort model based on a constant time headway, Nash equilibrium can be resolved through an extensive network search and relevant properties can be explored. Notably, employing Pontryagin's principle helps transform the problem into a more manageable form, facilitating both analytical and numerical analysis. Furthermore, employing a numerical algorithm to eliminate redundant variables yields an easier and more efficient solution.

This paper applies the composite gradient descent method in stochastic variational problems, focusing on predicting customer satisfaction in telecom. Previous studies have used stochastic gradients to solve machine learning problems, but this research demonstrates the practical convergence of composite gradients in real-world settings, where problem sizes are relatively small. Notably, CA-SGD outperforms SGD by improving convergence behavior and offers a 10% accuracy advantage, as shown in our analysis of Brazilian telecom data to identify the factors influencing customer satisfaction.

Recent research utilizing large language models indicates that these models can be employed to detect text provenance, an ability that poses significant challenges to proposed counter-measures for text authentication. This study, on the other hand, examines the ability of such models to distinguish between human-written and machine-generated content. Specifically, it focuses on transformer models' performance in identifying the difference between human authors and Transformer models as writers. While our results demonstrate that transformer models can accurately categorize the two groups, they also show that these models are incapable of evaluating the quality of transformer-generated text. Furthermore, we investigate the ability of transformer models to assess the coherence of text, discovering that these models can be used to flag incoherent news headlines resulting from Transformer model corruption processes.

Chiral spin liquids are an intriguing example of quantum entanglement, yet they are unlikely to occur in traditional materials, which are dominated by an even number of edges in their geometric structure. By modifying this constraint, researchers are exploring chiral spin liquids in materials with a high proportion of plaquettes having a odd number of edges, such as those found in quantum honeycomb lattices, chiral frustrated J1-J2 and Heisenberg models, and the Kagome model with magnetic field. Monte Carlo simulations reveal that these systems can have two types of entangled ground states, one with a small energy gap and another with a large gap. Notably, the small gap state is stable over a wide range of parameters and shares similarities with a spin-1/2 Chern insulator model. It exhibits a non-zero edge specific heat and localized excitations, unlike the large gap state, which is characterized by a large energy gap and localized excitations.

A novel method for calibrating large-antenna arrays in real-time is presented, utilizing the inverse matrix of the redundant antenna group's covariance matrix. Calibration occurs over time intervals of a few seconds to minimize the effects of antenna gain variations, which may occur every few seconds in this setup. A theoretical framework demonstrating the scheme's feasibility has been developed, which leverages the effects of diffuse interstellar gas and dust on different celestial sources. By calculating the cross-correlation between these gas/dust emissions, specific elements of the antenna group's covariance matrix can be derived, enabling accurate calibration. Furthermore, this approach allows for the derivation of the calibration process's variance, which is found to be inversely proportional to the number of redundant groups. Consequently, this method's performance can be optimized by selecting the appropriate band frequency and a large enough antenna group size. Furthermore, this method's variance can be reduced by a factor of 10 or more when applied to a 256-antenna antenna group, while maintaining angular resolution without the need for additional hardware.

We introduce the "autoencoding CGAN" (ACGAN) framework to automatically create a portfolio that minimizes risk while delivering a desired level of return. Through novel loss functions within the ACGAN, historical price data is mapped to return distributions, allowing for an optimal portfolio to be selected based on its expected returns and covariance, with expected returns and covariance controlled by a desired level of return. Our framework selects the portfolio that significantly deviates from the Markowitz's recommended allocation but meets the same return requirements. Our approach is verified using a real-world example with US market data, demonstrating its ability to provide superior portfolio returns with reduced risk.

Within the framework of the variable flavor number scheme, there is a need for the transition function $A_{gq}^{(3)}(N)$ to account for situations where a gluon evolves into a non-valence quark, necessitating a calculation in perturbation theory. This research derives the one-loop level of the three-loop approximation, known as $A_{qgq}^{(3)}(N)$, in a general dimension of space-time, using the Feynman integral method. This research also considers a related calculation for a different transition function, defined as $A_{qqq\bar{q}}^{(3)}(N)$, in which a non-valence quark evolves into a valence quark. This research concludes by presenting the five-loop level of the related transition function, defined as $A_{qgq}^{(4)}(N)$, in a reverse engineering form.

For classification tasks with small datasets marked by data imbalance, Bayesian neural networks are an optimal choice. While existing research has introduced methods for estimating Bayesian neural network outputs, these techniques are computationally expensive and impractical for the already challenging task at hand. To address this issue, we introduce a new approach called Bayesian ResNet, which adapts the standard residual neural network architecture to create a model capable of efficient approximation of complex functions. By parameterizing Bayesian residual neural networks using a Bayesian linear neural network, we are able to derive a Gaussian posterior distribution over the model's outputs. This posterior distribution can then be approximated using standard methods, making a significant reduction in computation possible. To validate our approach, we compare the accuracy of Bayesian ResNet with other methods in classification tasks with small and imbalanced datasets.

Social media platforms have become integral to people's daily lives, with user-generated content being a central feature. However, accessing the content generated by users, particularly that which is based on their interests, is often hindered by the user-driven nature of those systems. While algorithms can help, they often struggle to accurately determine users' interests. In contrast, group users' interests can be more easily detected by analyzing their collaborative behavior. This study investigates the feasibility of leveraging users' group interests to enhance user-generated content discovery and addresses two key challenges: (1) effectively utilizing group interests and (2) identifying users with shared interests. To address these challenges, we developed two algorithms, which are demonstrated to perform better than existing solutions in various scenarios. Specifically, our content discovery algorithm more accurately finds relevant, user-generated content, and our graph algorithm efficiently identifies users with shared interests.

This research aligns and expands upon the principles established in [10, 25], introducing certain modifications to the rules of the matrix join and the Hadamard product. The revised concepts initially apply to the computation of spectral properties of the matrix join of graphs. The join of graphs is a fundamental operation that combines two graphs by taking a graph and completely joining each of its vertices with the vertices of the other graph. The revised ideas then extend to the spectral analysis of the tensor join of weighted graphs. Furthermore, this study facilitates interactions between weighted graphs and their corresponding adjacency matrices. Additionally, this work has a broader implications for the computation of the spectral properties of weighted hypergraphs through the utilization of the hypergraph join operation.

INSIST is a groundbreaking, cost-effective imaging project led by the University of Oxford. The project successfully employs the Hubble Space Telescope, utilizing machine learning to enhance images captured by the low-resolution Wide Field Camera 3. By analyzing several high-quality images and comparing them to lower quality counterparts, the project demonstrates significant improvements achieved through the application of this enhanced imaging technique, effectively overcoming blurring caused by cosmic dust and other factors, while also correcting the impact of the telescope optics. The project successfully submitted an high-quality image of the Hubble Space Telescope itself, which is not possible using traditional methods. The INSIST project has made its code and images publicly available through GitHub and HubbleSite.org.

Recent advancements in medical research have significantly increased the demand for effective statistical tools to examine the impact of medical treatments on continuous outcomes in clinical trials. The current approach often relies on the application of constrained longitudinal data analysis paired with a two-stage least squares method, which, despite addressing some issues, comes with added analytical complexity and computational costs. This research introduces a novel hybrid method combining constrained longitudinal data analysis with a single-stage estimation using a natural cubic spline technique, which efficiently handles time trends and provides more accurate treatment effect estimates. The proposed method involves utilizing a natural cubic spline to estimate treatment effects and employing a constrained logistic regression to determine the treatment trend over time. The effectiveness of this approach is demonstrated through both a comprehensive clinical trial simulation and actual medical trial data analysis.

A key challenge in molecular simulations is efficiently exploring vast amounts of conformational space. A novel approach called conformational space annealing has shown success in sampling complex structures, but its application to reactions is limited due to the small number of reactive configurations. A proposed solution, Conformational Space Annealing with Reactions (CSAR), targets improving reaction pathway exploration by focusing on increasing the frequency of reactions and generating diverse reaction paths. CSAR's main objectives are to increase reaction frequency, generate abundant equilibrium configurations, and facilitate comprehensive sampling of conformational and potential energy landscapes. By utilizing a combination of energy minimization, enhanced sampling, and careful management of conformers, CSAR achieves its goals. In a test involving a model peptide, CSAR successfully identified the peptide's most efficient folding route and produced numerous stable structures.

This paper explores the relationship between specific estimates and types of parabolic and elliptic Hessian equations. The $L^{\frac{n}{n-1}}$ estimates are connected to one set of parabolic equations, while another set of estimates, known as the Gigena estimates, are related to a different set of parabolic equations. We also provide a method for transforming the original parabolic Hessian equation into an elliptic hyperbolic equation.

The simply typed lambda calculus with Church encodings for basic data types can be closely关联 to the simply typed lambda calculus with those encodings' type systems. This finding leads to a novel approach of enhancing lambda calculus with those encodings and corresponding type rules in an organized manner. This new method allows for the incorporation of more complex polynomial data types, such as those with multiple constructors and arbitrary subterm structures within the calculus. Additionally, this representation has been successfully applied to derive automated proof methods for their associated inductive type systems.

By employing a generalized version of Stein's theory, a weak derivative with respect to a measure is defined on path-space, and this derivative is utilized to derive the relationship between the integrals. The generalization involves extending the concept of derivatives to path-space, utilizing a given probability measure $\mu$, and this concept is utilized to establish a relationship between the integrals. The relationship can be extended to a class of functions, denoted as $\mathcal{C}_{\mu}^{1,b,m}(E\times\mathbb{R}^{d},m)$, and this extension is used to derive the relationship between the integrals. The generalization has significant implications in the context of forward Kolmogorov equations for path-space, and this concept is utilized to establish the relationship between the integrals. This paper draws connections between established mathematical concepts, specifically separation axioms and subspaces of compactness in topology, by relating them to the study of particular normal subgroups that feature a unique hull-kernel-type topology within group algebras of bounded type. Key examples of group algebras include the group algebras with bounded coefficients over certain fields and group C*-algebras.

This research introduces a novel framework that leverages knowledge graphs to generate complex SQL queries by translating natural language into graph representations. It employs a multi-stage process involving a graph generation module, a query generation module, and a self-correction module. Each stage is powered by transformer-based language models. The proposed framework stands out due to its ability to execute complex SQL queries without relying on actual database contents, thus achieving better execution accuracy by $10.56\%$. Furthermore, it facilitates explainability by outlining the graph's knowledge representation and enhancing performance through self-correction that refines both graph and query generations.

In this research, a novel approach to collision avoidance is proposed for multi-robot networks, where robots' future trajectories are predicted using recurrent neural networks. A probabilistic communication system between robots is implemented to share future trajectory forecasts, enabling each robot to share its uncertainty about its future path. In this setup, inter-robot messages are assumed to be independent of each robot's future trajectory, leading to a new communication error prediction error (CEPE) metric that integrates prediction errors into the decision-making process. The CEPE metric is then integrated into a probabilistic communication and estimation-aware model predictive control (PEC-EAPE) framework. By minimizing a risk function that includes a prediction error variance, this approach ensures safe robot behavior, even in situations where robot trajectories are uncertain. The proposed PEC-EAPE framework is evaluated through a multi-robot simulation, where results show that this approach outperforms a traditional model predictive control method that doesn't take prediction errors into account.

We have conducted a kinematic study of Andromeda XXv, the smallest galaxy of its kind orbiting the Andromeda galaxy. Our study of this ultra-faint dwarf galaxy, the second known of its kind to orbit an Andromeda galaxy, involved the collection of 17 new stellar velocities using high-resolution spectroscopy. Our data yielded 29 velocity measurements, the most for Andromeda XXv, and we have used these to determine its properties. Our findings show that the galaxy has an extremely low mass-to-light ratio of 100 to 1,000 times the sun's, and it contains a very small amount of dark matter. Our research also suggests that this galaxy has a radius of about 210 light years and contains a population of stars that has not been affected by processes of star formation or destruction. Moreover, we have found that this galaxy's population of stars is extremely metal-poor, the second known case of its kind to orbit the Andromeda galaxy. Our data indicates that the galaxy's population of stars is not uniform and may have been affected by a process of stripping by the Andromeda galaxy. Our research also shows that the galaxy's population of stars is not uniform and may have been formed in a small, isolated cluster.
