Our method, based on the renormalization group, systematically addresses mass-dependent issues arising in the context of heavy quarks and their impact on the theories of lighter, non-abelian flavors. This strategy facilitates a more comprehensive understanding of the effects of large mass ratios on the QCD coupling, enabling a multi-scale analysis of the QCD beta function. Furthermore, our approach allows for the accurate computation of higher-order corrections to the QCD coupling, thereby aiding in the assessment of theoretical uncertainties. Notably, our findings support the renormalization group incompressibility (RGIm) model, which offers a more precise and analytically based approach to the running QCD coupling. This approach may enable the identification of lower bounds on the QCD scale, $\Lambda_{QCD}^{(n)}$, with potential implications for the stability of hadronic matter.

Consider a finite, undirected graph G, denoted as G= (V, E), which is not necessarily connected, and let's define the degree of G as the maximum value of the degrees of the vertices in G, denoted $\Delta(G)$, minus the minimum value of the degrees of the vertices in G, denoted $\delta(G)$. A Fleischner's Conjecture holds that every 3-degenerate graph satisfies this inequality. This paper aims to modify this inequality by proving that every triangle-free graph satisfies this inequality.

We introduce a novel family of operators, known as shifted weighted shifted compression operators, linked to weighted Bergman spaces on the unit disk. Our findings reveal that these operators are compact under certain conditions, specifically when the weight with which functions are integrated into the norm decreases rapidly as they approach the boundary of the unit disk, while growth conditions allow for an increase. However, in instances where this pattern is reversed, these operators exhibit invariant subspaces of infinite codimension, thereby containing non-zero compact operators that have compressive properties within corresponding subspaces.

The emergence of the COVID-19 pandemic has led to a pressing need for effective diagnostic tools to detect the disease early. While previous studies have utilized chest X-rays and CT scans to identify COVID-19, they failed to account for the valuable insights that can be gained from analyzing lung tissue and integrating clinical information. Furthermore, previous approaches lacked transparency and interpretability. Our proposed solution involves a novel, end-to-end deep learning model called COVID-Net, which utilizes 3D convolutional operations to analyze CT scans and outperforms traditional 2D convolutional neural networks in terms of performance. Our analysis reveals that incorporating tissue segmentation and clinical data enhances the model's results. Specifically, the combination of these factors boosted our model's sensitivity to 90.1% and accuracy to 87.7%, classifying patients into five possible outcomes: COVID-19, Tuberculosis, Malignancy, Normal, or Pneumonia. To further improve interpretability, we have incorporated attention mechanisms into our model. Our findings demonstrate that our approach not only detects COVID-19 effectively but also identifies other respiratory conditions with comparable performance.

The surge in in-orbit satellites has led to a significant increase in space debris, making the future of satellite mega-constellations uncertain due to a growing number of inactive satellites. To address this challenge, the concept of minimum space occupancy (MiSO) orbits has been proposed as an innovative solution, featuring a bidirectional and interlinked setup that enables the monitoring of the entire space using a minimized number of satellites. This study utilizes a multi-objective optimization approach to enhance the design efficiency of MiSO mega-constellations and develop optimal configurations for satellite constellations with global coverage capabilities.

The use of typical parametric curves and surfaces in CAD models leads to intricate and detailed mesh patterns consisting of numerous quads. The creation of such quads often requires manual mesh generation, which can result in cluttered layouts that impede mesh processing algorithms. The application of T-meshes facilitates the automatic generation of quads with uncomplicated configurations, consisting of clusters, rows, and columns. Using a novel mesh generation technique based on parameter partitioning, three distinct T-mesh configurations can be derived from a particular surface, and these configurations can then be employed to create parametric meshes. The effectiveness of this method is demonstrated through various test cases, showing its ability to generate simplified and structured T-meshes, row, and column meshes, and the results of producing different quad layouts from T-meshes on specific CAD models.

This paper presents a theoretical framework for approximating p-values in the context of p-values calculated from test statistics that are not normally distributed in two dimensions. A two-step procedure is proposed for this purpose. The method initially involves fitting an elliptical distribution to the given data, followed by transforming this ellipse into a circle through projection, which enables estimation of p-values for test statistics of interest. Several elliptical and infinite divisibile distributions are examined, allowing for derivation of p-values of test statistics that do not conform to a normal, two-dimensional distribution. Moreover, a procedure to calibrate these p-values is developed, allowing for adjustments to better align with true, asymptotic p-values based on the elliptical distributions. Moreover, a procedure to calibrate these p-values is developed, allowing for adjustments to better align with true, asymptotic p-values based on the elliptical distributions. The method is demonstrated through examples of correlation coefficients and Mahalanobis distances, showcasing its ability to generate reasonably accurate p-value approximations across a range of scenarios. Additionally, the method is applied to approximate p-values for test statistics in multiple research areas, including those testing for independence, symmetry, and spherical distribution, as well as test statistics derived from linear combinations of random variables. Finally, a simulation study demonstrates the method's ability to generate reasonably accurate p-values across a range of scenarios, including cases where the method demonstrates little bias, as well as cases where the method demonstrates moderate bias, but bias reduction techniques can be applied

The quantum $S$-matrix theory holds promise as a black-hole quantum mechanics framework, offering potential in several key areas. The theory's applicability is particularly promising for certain classes of black-holes, characterized by specific horizon properties, as opposed to those with smooth-throat counterparts. The approach can be extended to post-Newtonian metrics and provides insights into black-hole mergers. The quantum $S$-matrix can also be adapted to describe non-spherically symmetric black-holes and offers a practical method for studying black-holes with smooth, flat regions. The application of this theory to cosmology and de Sitter metrics presents further possibilities, as seen in a proposed model for dark energy. The integration of quantum mechanics with general relativity in this context may yield new understanding of the universe's quantum nature, as seen in an $SU(2,2)$-inspired quantum-de-Sitter metric. The application of this theory to certain types of rotating black-holes and their specific properties, such as their rotation and potential singularities, also presents intriguing possibilities. The application of this theory to anti-de Sitter spaces and their specific properties, such as the presence of horizons, also offers a unique perspective on the universe. The application of this theory to specific types of rotating black-holes and their unique properties, such as the presence of singularities, also offers a new perspective on the nature of the universe.

This research explores the stabilization of Navier-Stokes dynamics using linear feedback controls, specifically targeting nearly steady situations that are inherently unstable in a half-space above a stationary plate. Unlike prior work that employed controls dependent on spatial area, this investigation utilizes controls confined to a thin layer near the unstable plate. The feedback control is designed by solving a related adjoint problem, with its influence restricted to an extremely narrow control zone that shrinks as a power law with respect to the power of the feedback parameter. The analysis reveals that this novel control structure is highly effective in achieving stabilization under certain parameter conditions.

Introducing the LitMind Dictionary that boasts a comprehensive collection of definitions in two languages, including Chinese and Lithuanian. This extensive dictionary comprises nearly 100,000 Chinese entries and a comparable number of Lithuanian entries with generated definitions leveraging advanced BERT models. The dictionary's development is accompanied by comprehensive analysis of its data, as well as a thorough evaluation of its capabilities and limitations in generating definitions and synonyms for complex words using smaller neural networks. The dictionary aims to facilitate interdisciplinary communication, particularly between Lithuanian and Chinese languages, and is freely accessible for download.

Recent advancements in post-hoc explanation methods have been pivotal in understanding complex non-linear recommendation models, yet they merely provide an after-the-fact explanation. Research indicates that models relying on post-hoc explanations may exhibit lower robustness compared to explanation-aware models. To address this limitation, we introduce the Recurrent Crispr model, an innovative approach that incorporates post-hoc explanation-awareness into its recommendation framework. The Recurrent Criskr model, a post-hoc explanation-aware recurrent model, is composed of two interconnected components - the Recurrent Crispr Gate Network and the Recurrent Crispr Editor Network. The former, inspired by gene editing technology, ensures that the recommended items are easily understandable through its activation pattern. The latter, grounded in recurrent neural networks, facilitates the learning of meaningful representations. By incorporating post-hoc explanation-awareness, the proposed model achieves superior recommendation performance and is validated through comprehensive evaluations on real-world datasets.

In the In$_{0.29}$Al$_{0.71}$InP/InP system, the unique band structure of the InP outer layers results in a fixed Fermi level position, which is relatively high and close to the edge of the conduction band. This leads to a pronounced two-dimensional electron gas (2D electron gas) at the interface with a relatively high electron density. To address this challenge and manipulate the surface Fermi level, researchers have incorporated a thin layer composed of In$_{0.81}$Al$_{0.19}$InP and Al$_{0.71}$InP$_{0.53}$, creating a double heterostructure. This novel approach, for the first time, successfully shifts the surface Fermi level to a lower position, closer to the edge of the valence band. A simulation based on the transfer matrix method revealed that the double heterostructure effectively confines the Fermi level at the outer interface and allows for the adjustment of electron density by altering the thickness of the InP spacers.

We have made significant advancements in understanding the distribution-free robust learning potential of various concept classes with uncertain parameters, revealing that robust learning is feasible when the query's radius exceeds a certain size but challenging when radius falls below a certain size. Specifically, we developed a general technique for distribution-free robust learning concept classes with finite VC-dimensions using queries offering a certain loss reduction, and also demonstrated the difficulty of such learning when using queries offering a certain loss reduction over infinite concept classes with a certain robust VC-dimension. Furthermore, we introduced specific constraints that limit the query's maximum radius while ensuring distribution-free robust learning potential for finite VC-dimension classes and highlighted a class of concepts where such potential exists without imposing a lower bound on the query's radius. In addressing the problem of robust classification without an oracle query, we proposed a general algorithm for learning concept classes with a certain VC-dimension and providing certain loss reduction and false positive rates. Lastly, in the context of robust clustering, we showed that various unique unique solutions exist and that they can be efficiently found through various general techniques.

The Fast Sinkhorn II (FS-2) algorithm is an optimized version of the Sinkhorn-Cottrell algorithm, incorporating a multi-grid framework and a finer-to-coarser strategy to tackle the computational complexity of optimal transport problems. Our investigation into FS-2 has involved a thorough examination through convergence analysis, experimentation, and benchmarking against other algorithms like the multi-grid UMAP algorithm to solve optimal transport within geometric deep learning applications.

Our research focuses on the mass loss from AU Mic b, a 1.1 Jupiter-mass exoplanet orbiting the flaring M-star AU Mic. We conducted observations of the AU Mic system using the Magellan telescope and the NIRSPEC instrument, which is equipped with a camera. Our study analyzed data from 18 observations and simulated flares based on previous studies. We found that the mass loss from AU Mic b is minimal in quiescent state but increases by a factor of 10-100 during stellar flares. Our simulations confirmed that our findings are in line with current understanding of planetary mass loss.

We explore how particle movement affects the curvature of matter and the resulting force, which is analogous to radiation friction, but with a variational form and radiation-based interpretation. The outcome reveals that a particle's self-consistent field includes a form of radiation "friction" and dynamic "momentum." Subsequently, the equations of motion based on this field lead to analogous results to classical mechanics when the particle dynamics are derived using variational principles. Furthermore, the established field of radiation "friction" demonstrates a direct link to a form of radiation "energy." Notably, this approach indicates that a particle's field can be interpreted as a resistive medium that impedes the particle's acceleration, thereby causing the particle to lose energy as radiation.

This paper presents novel algorithms for addressing the issue of imbalanced data classification. Our approach involves utilizing existing knowledge from similar data sets and oversampling minority class samples in a data-efficient manner, unlike traditional methods such as SMOTE and ADASYN which rely on generating minority samples from randomly selected majority samples. Our methods incorporate both a data-level approach and a decision-level approach, resulting in enhanced performance and reduced computational complexity when handling minority class samples.

A comprehensive survey, called the Southern Spectroscopic QSO Hunt (SSQh), has been conducted to identify and discover previously unknown Southern QSOs.  The investigation involved a series of observations using the Magellan telescopes and utilized data from 2018 to 2020.  The study utilized three distinct methods of obtaining spectra, including those with and without preliminary identification via low-resolution spectra or imaging.  The research resulted in the discovery of 130 QSOs, of which 127 have a magnitude of $19.5$ or greater and 3 are marginal.  The study also reports on 29 previously reported objects, of which 13 are confirmed as QSOs, and 20 new non-QSO sources, primarily consisting of galaxies and galaxies.  The study presents the first catalog of QSOs, which includes 130 newly discovered QSOs and 40 QSOs from previous research, observed between 2015 and 2020.  The catalog also provides a comprehensive list of data, such as right ascension, magnitude, magnitude, redshift, and redshift.  The study further provides information on the distribution of QSOs in the southern hemisphere and discusses the characteristics of the field QSOs, which are not part of a known galaxy.

A quantum dot can act as an effective tool to study the addition spectrum of a superconductor through hybrid experiments combining the dot with a superconducting material. The experiment operates by employing resonant voltage excitation of the dot, in conjunction with a constant bias on the superconductor, to selectively probe specific addition energies and characterize electron-phonon interactions. Additionally, a strong magnetic field can be applied to either a) selectively eliminate high addition energies by restricting the interaction between electron-like and hole-like excitations with phonons, or b) reduce the addition energies by lowering the energy gap between these two exactions. These field manipulations enable a deeper understanding of the dot's unique properties and may lead to novel electronic devices that combine quantum dots with superconductors.

It is established that the class of intermediate shocks in two-dimensional isotropic magnetohydrodynamics contains a contraction operator, provided a certain measure is taken. This is accompanied by the definition of an appropriate entropic measure. Additionally, a specific contractive property is proven for that measure. However, this is found to be inconsistent with the entropy measure used in prior research by Guo and Xu.

Deep learning has made significant advancements in understanding scenes captured in a single image, with techniques like perpetual view generation gaining momentum due to their potential applications. Nonetheless, the task of generating a sequence of perspectives from a single input remains an unresolved challenge. To address this issue, we've developed a novel approach that leverages existing data, enabling the generation of intricate scenes in novel views. To assess the effectiveness of this method, we've created a comprehensive dataset featuring a wide variety of scenes and perspectives, surpassing existing benchmarks. Through comparative analyses with existing approaches, we've found our method produces high-quality, novel views and demonstrates robust generalization to scenes not seen during training.

The application of model predictive control (MPC) to large complex network systems poses significant computational challenges, primarily due to the extensive model linearization required to incorporate constraints. The use of machine learning techniques, particularly the Koopman operator theory, presents a viable solution to this issue, enabling the use of a linear MPC controller despite the underlying system's nonlinearity. The proposed approach combines the global Koopman operator with a local approximation to mitigate the model linearization issue, thus allowing for the efficient control of large-scale systems. The proposed method involves two stages: first, estimating the Koopman operator globally using the Volterra series and kernel regression and the identified spectral variables; second, incorporating the estimated spectral variables into the control constraints to generate a linear MPC controller. The effectiveness of this approach is demonstrated through the simulation of a nonlinear power system.

We utilize a two-dimensional quasi-one-dimensional model to simulate the dynamics of liquid films forming around fibres. This simulation occurs within a frame that moves at the same speed as the fibres, which are positioned in an extended, stationary bath of liquid. On fibres with radii less than 10 micrometres, and relative speeds below 100 centimetres per second, our model reveals a striking occurrence of periodic droplets and waves on advancing films. To explain this phenomenon theoretically, we extend the lubrication theory to incorporate the periodic variations in film thickness caused by these droplets. Our simplified model demonstrates that droplet sizes and spacings conform to a specific law, which we verify against simulations that employ detailed surface tension calculations. Notably, this validation holds true even for fibres with varying boundary conditions at their surface, showcasing the model's versatility and robustness.

We examine the behavior of a Lyapunov exponent in a specific geometric model, derived from Jacobian flows and their associated Lagrangian metrics, as the parameter $\sigma$ approaches zero. The results demonstrate that the behavior of this metric and the corresponding exponent under strong contraction ($\sigma \to 0$) is governed by the distribution of particles, mapped from Lagrangian to Eulerian coordinates, rather than the metrics and coordinates themselves. The analysis reveals that the exponential growth rate of certain specific lengths in the Lagrangian metric, under the given contraction, is either infinite or zero and is uniquely determined by the distribution of points $\xvec$. The analysis, based on earlier work by Gol\'es and Skibba, builds upon key ideas of previous researchers including Ledrappier, Hunt, and Reiss, and involves a new derivation of a metric in Lagrangian coordinates. The methods employed can be applied to solve the inverse problem of determining the divergence rate of particle spacings, given the particles' spatial distribution.

Scoliosis, a condition characterized by an irregular curvature of the spine, is often studied through various techniques. Recent developments in robotic ultrasound technology have made it possible to track the movement of spine processes in real-time and to study the behavior of scoliosis patients in different situations. Determining the location of spinous processes is a key challenge, and researchers have developed techniques to calculate the angles between adjacent processes. To assess the reliability of this method, researchers conducted a study and found that the standard deviation of the calculated angles was less than 1.5 degrees, and that the method yields accurate results comparable to those of a radiologist. Consequently, the study suggests that using ultrasound to monitor scoliosis patients may be a viable option for further investigation.

This paper presents a new duration modeling approach and validates its feasibility.
A key distinction from conventional methods lies in our novel algorithm, which
calculates discrete duration distributions without making assumptions about their
underlying continuous distributions. The proposed method involves transforming
a given duration variable into a latent space where regression can be applied,
followed by a discretization step to generate the duration distribution. To
evaluate a duration model, we introduced measures based on distribution similarity
and used these metrics to assess various models, our results reveal that several
models consistently fail, one model marginally improves performance, and our
approach consistently yields the best outcomes.

This study examines the potential of using AI to automatically detect and prevent hate speech on social media platforms, particularly Facebook. To achieve this, we developed a unique approach that leverages linguistic and semantic features, along with traditional machine learning models, to identify online posts containing hate speech. By combining these features, we were able to achieve a classification accuracy of 91.01%, demonstrating that the proposed method is both efficient and reliable in identifying hate speech online. In comparison, the deep learning model achieved an accuracy of 85.89%, while the traditional machine learning model's accuracy ranged between 91.01% and 96.28%, signifying that the proposed approach outperforms these models in identifying online hate speech.

In this work, a novel unmixing approach is presented as a key component of the Multiple Input Multiple Output (MIMO) unmixing framework. The MIMO unmixing method attempts to tackle the issue of sparsity in MIMO mixing matrices by solely relying on marginal information from the observed data. Nonetheless, a significant shortcoming of the MIMO unmixing method is its tendency to fail in subnetworks composed of sparse matrices, as subnetworks are commonly present in the data being unmixed due to the underlying composition of smaller mixing matrices, especially in cases where these smaller networks are non-trivial. The issue is addressed by introducing an unmixing step designed to tackle non-sparse or non-sparse-plus-noise characteristics, which are observed in subnetworks. The integration of this unmixing method with the existing MIMO unmixing procedure significantly enhances its overall performance. The proposed unmixing approach is based on the concept that a network's "plus noise" configuration is characterized by a shift in its output, as opposed to the non-sparse configuration. The unmixing method is further refined to be more exact, as it borrows the idea of the non-sparse configuration and superimposes it onto the "plus noise" configuration. The outcome of the unmixing process, as demonstrated in the work, reveals that the refined method exhibits a higher degree of accuracy in comparison with the original MIMO unmixing method.

Document analysis involves analyzing historical documents like handwritten letters, 
diaries, and news articles to extract specific information. However, identifying 
relevant datasets to develop effective document structures is a time-consuming and 
challenging task. Our objective is to facilitate the discovery of suitable datasets 
by creating a search engine that can be accessed through a user-friendly web interface. 
The document structure search engine (DocStr Search) uses a combination of techniques 
to match document structures with relevant datasets based on visual and textual comparisons. 
Our experiments show that the proposed method is effective in ranking datasets 
according to their correlation with the target document structure. The DocStr Search 
tool is available online through its public demo interface.

To comply with a compliant tool that has been installed on a robot's end-effector, the robot needs to be able to follow the predetermined path exactly. To achieve this, we adapted an advanced control technique, called computed and torque control, to control a robot that is working with a compliant tool. To increase the robot's tracking accuracy, the control law takes into account the dynamics of the compliant tool and uses real-time force measurements to adjust the control input in a feedback loop. By applying this approach to a six-degree-of-fredom compliant tool that is being used to apply force to a flexible material, we found that it results in much better tracking accuracy. To ensure the control technique is efficient and effective, we developed an optimal control law and used simulation to test its performance.

The long-term impact of myocardial infarction (MI) on individuals' health is significant and diverse, extending beyond the initial event itself. To study how chronic conditions following MI are linked over time and their socio-demographic influences, researchers used data from the UK's Electronic Health Records and applied advanced statistical methods to a diverse group of people who experienced MI between 2005 and 2014. The analysis, which involved over 70,000 individuals, used a statistical model to identify linked conditions over time, and over 1 million diagnoses were recorded. The study's findings showed that certain long-term conditions, such as diabetes and depression, are more likely to be linked to other chronic diseases, and this pattern can be influenced by socio-demographic factors like gender, ethnicity, and location. The differences in healthcare utilization and coding practices may also affect the study's results. Overall, the study highlights the importance of considering chronic conditions as part of a continuous timeline, which can reveal more nuanced patterns of disease progression and their social influences.

To address potential issues with integrals involving the electronic continuum, a customized version of Becke's scheme is proposed for computing local correlation energies more reliably. While originally developed to tackle problems with real-space integrals, this modified approach is now applied to momentum-space integrals calculating these energies. By replacing the standard grid with a more suitable representation, either in the real- or reciprocal-space, significant improvements in both convergence and the accuracy of computed energies are observed. To leverage this enhanced approach, an analytical expression for Becke composite weighting functions in momentum space is derived for Gaussian-type orbital models. Extensive testing demonstrates that incorporating this weighting function leads to substantially improved convergence, particularly when employing representations that employ purely s-p-d-g basis functions.

Building upon the concept of metric dimension introduced by Harary and Harary, researchers have explored parameterized complexity with various graph parameters and nearly complete results obtained so far. However, the application of metric dimension remains limited in graph theory due to a lack of results tied to fundamental graph invariants. This study aims to investigate the parameterized complexity of the Metric Dimension problem parameterized by graph parameters. We focus on ten parameters, employing established techniques and introducing a novel approach based on the Lipton-Rosenberg theorem. Our findings show that Metric Dimension is fixed-parameter tractable under certain conditions and parameterized wreath-hard when parameterized by other variables. Additionally, we have identified the minimum achievable kernel size for Metric Dimension and determined its precise kernel size.

For the category of directed spaces, which extends dcpos with the Scott topology by incorporating a continuous function with the inverse property, we define upper, lower, and convex powerspaces. Although the powerspaces of dcpos are established, our analysis shows that the powerspaces of directed spaces differ significantly due to the additional requirement. By proving that the powerspaces are directed spaces and have specific fixed point sets, we also demonstrate that the powerspaces have distinct homotopy types compared to their dcpos equivalents.

In lower-tropospheric hothouse climates with extensive cloud cover, the maximum temperature is kept below the maximum emission temperature by thick clouds, which have low water vapor permeability and restrict the water vapor concentration, in line with the climate of a standard Earth with much higher water vapor permeability. In the case of thin clouds, the water vapor permeability is comparable to that of the standard Earth climate. In both the hothouse and standard Earth climates with extensive cloud cover, the average water vapor concentration in the clear areas is at the saturation point. In hothouse climates with extensive cloud cover, the clear areas tend to experience more precipitation due to increased atmospheric instability and cloudless areas, which in turn generate more precipitation, although the presence of hothouse clouds may lead to cloud-top precipitation. In contrast to the clear areas, lowland clouds tend to be less prevalent in highland clouds, which in turn leads to the concentration of cloudless areas and increased average cloud fraction. In contrast to the lowland clouds, highland clouds tend to be present even in hothouse climates with less extensive cloud fraction. In hothouse climates with moderate to thick clouds, the surface temperature tends to be lower than in standard Earth climates. In hothouse climates with thin clouds, the surface temperature tends to be lower than in standard Earth climates, whereas the temperature at the top of the lowest cloud layer is comparable to the maximum emission temperature. To describe quantum gravity, we suggest a novel higher-spin extension of Yang-Mills theory characterized by a gauge action involving Chern-Simons terms, potential solutions of which encompass theories with independent spin greater than one and may represent higher-spin counterparts to Chern-Simons theories.

A deep neural network-based binary classifier is compromised by an adversary who can create and disseminate a vast number of adversarial samples, causing significant accuracy loss in a large dataset. To counter this issue, we introduce the concept of label refurbishment, which enables a deep neural network to acquire robustness against adversarial samples. Recently, the in-label refurbishment method (ILRM) was proposed, but its scope of label refurbishment was restricted to only samples within a specified proximity to a given label. In this paper, we present an advanced version of ILRM called the Bayesian statistics guided label refurbishment mechanism (BLRM), which expands its scope to encompass all labels and utilizes Bayesian statistics to determine a probability distribution over potential label refurbishments. Through a series of experiments conducted on multiple noisy datasets, we demonstrate that BLRM is highly effective and can significantly enhance the accuracy of deep neural networks.

We develop an advanced method for approximating functions in the unit cube using multivariate polynomials, based on interpolation at specific points within the space. Our approach builds on a fundamental identity for determining coefficients and utilizes basis polynomials derived from Chebyshev equations, which enable us to establish key properties of the resulting approximation method. By selecting nodes according to specific conditions, we are able to prove the existence of non-degenerate geometric configurations and leverage this to develop bounds for Christoffel coefficients. This bound, combined with the basis polynomials, enables us to prove convergence rates for approximations of bounded variation and Lipschitz functions.

The probability distribution of particles undergoing a correlated random walk can be calculated precisely in one dimension and nine dimensions when the correlation is limited to their immediate predecessors. In higher dimensional spaces, this precision is maintained as long as the correlation is restricted to a hypercube-shaped previous state space. These calculations yield closed-form expressions for the characteristic polynomial of the transition probability matrix for 1, 2 correlated, 9 correlated and 9 correlated previous by cube scenarios. Furthermore, the asymptotic behavior of the probability of a particle's location in these dimensions is derived and found to be influenced by the eigenvalues of the correlation matrix.

Non-deterministic clocks are a versatile tool for handling complex termination conditions in sophisticated algorithms. They allow the creation of termination proofs for functions with intricate logic, such as "n" items being processed with an auxiliary parameter "m" that may or may not correlate. In such cases, non-deterministic clocks can be utilized in a function's co-recursive auxiliary to minimize "m" without impacting its primary goal of reducing "n". We have developed a new, efficient method for proving termination in co-recursive types that avoids "m" decreasing monotonically, by incorporating generalized well-founded relations. We have further refined this approach to streamline the proof process, by introducing special mechanisms and automated reasoning techniques. Using our current tool, Calore, we have demonstrated the effectiveness of these refinement strategies on numerous examples, including an implementation of non-deterministic query optimization.

The 'hairpin' concept has been a cornerstone in modeling wall-bounded turbulence for over five decades, influencing RANS models and driving understanding of near-wall flow behavior through experimental and direct numerical simulation evidence. This review explores the origins and subsequent research on the hairpin concept, covering its presence across a spectrum of wall-bounded currents and for various phases of near-wall turbulence structures.

A simplified version of the Skyrme model, a theoretical framework for understanding particle interactions, has been expanded to include gauge effects.  By transforming to a specific coordinate system, the model can be reduced to basic wave equations.  These equations can take three distinct soliton forms – Gaussian wave packets, damped oscillations, and Jost solitons.  The analysis of this simplified model sheds light on significant issues within the fully developed Skyrme model.  The success in obtaining soliton solutions for the expanded model suggests a potential approach to introducing gauge effects into baby Skyrme models in future research.

We analyze the topological phases of a lattice-based Weyl semimetal model and a corresponding massless Dirac fermi gas to study the effects of dimensionality and crystal symmetry. The lattice-based Weyl semimetal model lacks inherent preference for any crystal symmetry but under specific parameters it exhibits a highly symmetric Weyl fermi state. In contrast, when the model is applied to a crystal lattice it breaks this symmetry resulting in various topological phases dependent on the chosen crystal symmetry. Specifically, when the crystal lattice possesses certain symmetries it allows for Weyl fermimetal, axion insulator and $\mathbb{Z}_2$ metal phases. Moreover, our investigation reveals that upon introducing interactions between fermions certain symmetry-rich crystals can host an unusual topological superconducting state with chiral Majorana edge modes at zero magnetic field due to spontaneous ferromagnetism.

Two nanoapertures in a double split ring structure can be adjusted to control
optical modes separately by modifying the spectral positions and intensities of
longitudinal and transverse resonances. A magnetic dipole generates the
longitudinal mode, induced by spectral patterns of electric dipole moments in
the two apertures facing each other. The transverse mode is generated by a
higher-order electric quadrupole due to spectral patterns of two facing parallel
electric dipoles and a longitudinal magnetic dipole. By adjusting the magnetic
dipole and electric quadrupole, both modes can be controlled simultaneously.

The sudden, sudden-like movements, or plastic events, in structured, crystal-like materials significantly impact their overall mechanical behavior. To gain a clearer understanding of the characteristics and frequency of these plastic events, researchers have established various methods for detecting and categorizing them. Recently, researchers have employed on-the-fly plastic event detection using a technique based on sudden changes in material density, or local variance. This new method shows remarkable consistency in results when compared to other techniques. Moreover, researchers have discovered that this local variance technique effectively highlights distinct characteristics in both completely ordered and partially ordered materials. When applied to various types of plastic events detected through different methods, researchers have found that they typically occur within relatively small, localized areas. Interestingly, researchers have found that less complex events often form larger clusters, regardless of their size.

The effect of Mn decoration on silicene's electronic properties was studied, specifically when placed at silicon sites in different ways: 
covering every site and random individual sites with a coverage of 1/3 and 1/4. By using density functional theory with dynamical mean-field theory, it was found that when Mn covers every site, the effective interaction parameter is stronger than in random decoration, and it's particularly strong when decorating only half of the sites every other site. This results in different phases being possible, such as a Mott insulating phase at specific electron densities, and it's predicted that optimal conditions for these phases can be found by adjusting parameters like tunneling and random coverage. This optimal coverage appears to be around 1/3, and it's promising for potential applications in spintronics due to its proximity to metal-insulator transition.

Recent observations of Sgr A* have revealed the supernova Sgr A East, which exploded approximately 3.4 parsecs away from the center of the galaxy. A series of VLA observations between 1977 and 1978 provided key observations of Sgr A East at 5 GHz, revealing a complex radio source with a central bright region and a radio halo extending up to 2 arcseconds. A comprehensive study of Sgr A East's radio emission between 1978 and 2020 has shown a significant increase in non-thermal radio emission by a factor of 3-4, which is likely caused by the interaction of the supernova remnant with the circumnuclear disk. A model based on radiative shock emission provides a satisfactory explanation for these radio observations.

This study examines the effects of class imbalance on the performance of classification techniques. A thorough evaluation of three algorithms, specifically k-nearest neighbors (KNN), support vector machines (SVM), and neural networks, reveals that class imbalance significantly impacts the effectiveness of KNN and SVM methods but has a lesser effect on the performance of neural networks. These findings motivated the development of a new, neural network-based approach to address class imbalance issues. Through experiments, we demonstrate that this approach can enhance the accuracy of neural networks in identifying the minority class at no additional computational cost.

This research introduces a comprehensive dataset of US state-specific local news coverage regarding the COVID-19 pandemic, consisting of 1.1 million articles from 4,700 local news outlets over 311 days. Building upon a large-scale web search and automated filtering process initiated on January 21, a crowdsourcing effort supplemented this data, collected from February 21 to March 21, encompassing articles from 46 additional states. Our study demonstrates the utility of this dataset by examining the evolution of COVID-19 reporting across time, state populations, and local news sources, emphasizing the impact of state case counts, outbreak onsets, and resource types on article volume, lengths, and topic diversity. Our research also reveals correlations between article topics, describing 58.5% as news, with the remaining coverage focusing on opinion, services, or other categories.

We have created a Fast Multipole Method algorithm written in CUDA for use with AMR-CL, a CUDA-based, adaptive-clustering tree code. Our implementation integrates with the existing AMR-CL library, allowing it to calculate the gravitational potential and force between particles efficiently, a typical task in astrophysical simulations. The CUDA method computes interactions between specific particle groups beyond a certain distance, significantly speeding up the computation. Our tests, using 128 to 8192 nodes, show a substantial 10-30% time savings over direct calculation, with near-perfect linear scaling across the tested range.

The ALICE experiment at the CERN LHC has recently provided a novel approach for measuring double spin asymmetry at very high energies by analyzing elastic electron-proton scattering events in proton-lead collisions. These events can occur on both the photon from the electron and the longitudinal spin of the proton. By analyzing these events, the team was able to determine the elastic electron-proton cross-section, which matches existing theoretical predictions. Moreover, the positive double spin asymmetry measured confirms that the photon-proton interaction is a dominant process in the elastic proton collision.

Behavior cloning, a fundamental approach in imitation learning, faces a significant challenge in effectively transferring expert behavior to student policies for complex control problems. Our proposed augmented policy cloning method seeks to overcome this limitation by integrating image-based actions from an expert with state features generated through visual question answering. This integration enables the student policy to rely on state features that are specifically designed for the task at hand, rather than relying solely on image-based actions, which can be unreliable. To address the challenge of determining the most appropriate action, we employ a multi-class classification task that asks the student policy to choose the correct action from a list of possible options. This method is demonstrated on complex robotic manipulation tasks and achieves significant improvements in performance, particularly in scenarios involving high-dimensional control problems.

A novel search method for discovering neutral heavy scalar or pseudoscalar particles has been introduced, focusing on associated production of these particles along with a Higgs boson, generated through a vector boson fusion process. The Higgs boson decays into two bottom quarks, while the other vector boson becomes off-shell and transforms into the neutral scalar or pseudoscalar particle through a loop of top and bottom quarks. This search utilizes the distribution of invariant mass formed by the Higgs boson and the heavy scalar or pseudoscalar particle, as well as the maximum transverse momentum of the vector bosons, to establish significant distinguishing factors. The studied scalars can have masses between 500 and 2000 GeV, with Higgs bosons possessing a mass of 125.25 GeV.

The nuclear spin maser, known for its exceptional spin sensitivity and ultra-low noise in frequency detection, has seen its design optimized by the incorporation of digital signal processing. Through the use of digital techniques, the spin maser's output can be efficiently detected, yielding notable improvements in its performance characteristics. Our study focuses on the spin maser's behavior under the influence of electromagnetic noise and a weak signal, and compares its sensitivity to that of the conventional lock-in amplifier and the dynamical nuclear polarization-enhanced lock-in amplifier. Our results indicate that the ENMR can achieve better signal-to-noise ratios and faster signal detection rates than the traditional lock-in amplifier in certain scenarios, a benefit that can be further amplified when combined with the DNPE.

Hypergeometric groups can be employed to investigate the self-transformations of K3 surfaces. By connecting the minimal K3 surface's dynamical properties to hyperbolic geometry, we can deduce the existence of specific self-transformations. This method was used to discover new K3 surface automorphisms and verify previously conjectured ones, including orders 13, 15, 16 and 32.

A new, "dark sector" neutralino state, originating from a standard neutralino, could decay into a lower-mass hidden neutralino and a gamma ray, potentially detectable by the Fermi Large Area Telescope (Fermi-LAT). Within certain parameter ranges, this decay could produce characteristic gamma ray signals in the cosmic gamma ray background spectrum, displaying a specific shape defined by two parameters. These parameters can be used to narrow down the search for these new states using data from gamma ray observations.

We propose a novel approach to compute the graph genus and near-miss invariants,
such as cross number and fractional genus. This is achieved by exploring all possible
exploration trees of sized sized vertices, up to surface isomorphism, for each possible
genus up to a predetermined limit, identifying the lowest possible graph embedding. The
result is an optimized and comprehensive algorithm, which, thanks to a clever use of
families of graphs, can be applied to all possible graphs of up to 40 vertices,
yielding the exact genus of these graphs, or a near-miss bound of plus three.

This study introduces two novel variations of conditional gradient stochastic optimization methods that allow for substantial savings in the number of communication rounds required. By utilizing variance-reduction techniques, these algorithms can terminate earlier when the variance of the local objective function gradients decreases over time. A crucial property is the localization of the objective function gradient, enabling servers to calculate the local gradient from local objectives without needing to share data. By leveraging this information in a deterministic variant, we achieve a variance-reduced estimator of the objective gradient, reducing the number of communication rounds by the square root of the ratio between the desired loss and the initial loss. Furthermore, we establish theoretical performance guarantees for both conditioned and localized variants, showing them to be superior to current state-of-the-art methods by reducing the number of communication rounds required, especially in scenarios with low condition number ratios and larger problem sizes.

To reduce the substantial training requirements for language models in low-resource languages, we explore the application of transfer learning for languages that share a historical connection. We examine three scenarios: (i) transfer between languages of the same family but different subgroups, specifically from Romance to Slavic languages; (ii) transfer between languages of the same subgroup, such as from Italian to Czech; and (iii) transfer between languages with the same developmental stage, such as from Italian to Spanish. We compare our results with direct training for target languages and with other forms of transfer learning involving non-related languages. We utilize the multilingual BERT model, which demonstrates transfer learning's effectiveness in improving low-resource languages through training on resources from their linguistic relatives.

A crucial aspect of dark matter research involves the ability to differentiate between signals generated by electrons and those resulting from nuclear interactions in detector materials. This process, known as recoil discrimination, is a fundamental challenge in detecting dark matter directly. Traditionally, the distinction between these two types of recoils has been made using the detector's pulse shape or the ratio of scintillation to ionization signals. We have developed a machine learning approach that utilizes newly discovered properties to enhance the efficiency of Gaseous Time Projection Chambers in distinguishing between electron and nuclear recoil signals. By training a neural network on ten engineered and natural electron recoil characteristics, in addition to the conventional S2/S1 ratio used in XENON and LUX-ZAP experiments, we have achieved a significant improvement in electron recoil discrimination capabilities. This innovation results in nearly a tenfold increase in the detector's ability to distinguish between electron and nuclear recoil signals while maintaining a very low level of misclassification for nuclear recoil signals.

This study presents a novel approach to evaluating external driver behavior by leveraging expert opinion and contextual behavior patterns. Building upon recent findings that highlight the significance of outside factors in contributing to collisions, our methodology involves a structured expert input phase followed by the creation of generic models based on observed contextual behavior. A demonstration of our approach was conducted in conjunction with an Italian insurance company, focusing on real-world data and specific traffic scenarios. Initially, an expert provided a structured knowledge framework outlining relevant external conditions and associated risk levels. Subsequently, a neural network model was trained to predict these conditions and associated risk levels from real data. A comparison with a conventional scoring system revealed enhanced performance and reduced discrepancies between predicted and actual scores.

We introduce a new scenario text recognition approach, referred to as CRAFT. CRAFT employs a multi-stage architecture comprising an initial text instance and vocabulary discovery component, followed by series models for encoding, recognition, and adaptation. To enhance the model's ability to discover novel OOV text instances and adapt to real-world environments, an innovative dataset and evaluation framework, referred to as "Out-Of-Vocabulary," have been created and proposed. CRAFT achieves impressive text recognition accuracy, surpassing the state-of-the-art with significant margins, and an ablation study validates the efficacy of the innovative components. Furthermore, the CRAFT model surpasses another leading model, Awen, in speed, and both models are now being hosted on a GitHub repository, available at https://github.com/tinghuazheng/CRAFT.

The Kozak-Popovich-Williams test is employed to assess the similarity between two random fields of different types by measuring their convergence. The process involves dividing the observation time into intervals of fixed duration and calculating the time-averaged increment vectors for each interval. The probability distribution of the maximum increment over these intervals is then calculated, as well as a metric called the relative deviation between the two random fields. The probability of this relative deviation exceeding a certain threshold is determined, as an indicator of convergence. The article examines the asymptotic properties of the test when applied to two classes of processes: the Strauss process and a two-dimensional Brownian motion with a time-dependent drift.

In the laboratory setting, magnetic levitation allows the creation of a seemingly weightless droplet within a fluid. When the fluid is quiescent and subject to a magnetic field, the initial disturbance is minimized. However, as time progresses, the droplet is subject to a Stokes drag force and begins to sink slowly, also causing buoyancy to shift the droplet laterally, resulting in its circular trajectory. For the specific case of drops and bubbles, surface tension and internal pressure can counteract the deformation of the droplet or bubble, making their dynamics mathematically tractable and, under a certain condition related to the magnetic to capillary number, analytically solvable.

We demonstrate that Hecke L-functions of primitive forms for SL2(Z), which exhibit a known connection to Hecke eigenforms of their central series counterparts, diverge when considered against the patterns set by cuspidal Hecke eigenforms of Spn(Z). This discrepancy holds true for Spn(Z), where the patterns set by cuspidal eigenforms remain unexplained by Riemann Hypothesis and the Generalized Riemann Man Hypothesis. Moreover, the observed phenomenon is not unique to Spn(Z), but also arises in the context of Hecke eigenforms of GL2(A_Q) and its connection to Sp1(Z).

In a normal graphene junction, we investigate the transport characteristics of systems consisting of two leads connected to a finite-size, doped, and gated graphene sheet. The transport quantities exhibit distinct behavior due to the unique electronic structure of graphene, differing significantly from that of conventional two-dimensional electron gases. The current-voltage relationships show strong, non-monotonic dependencies on various system parameters, including voltage, Fermi energy, conductance, and the doping level of the graphene. The underlying transport phenomena are governed by specific configurations of the graphene tight-binding bands, leading to intricate patterns of forward and reverse current flow. The analysis also reveals resistance plateaus and non-reciprocal behavior under specific conditions.

Weakly nonlinear and monotone operators in the context of Banach lattices exhibit convergent behavior under certain conditions, specifically in the norm topology and a weaker topology. This characteristic extends its applicability to weakly nonlinear coherent laws among weakly increasing sequences of monotone random operators. As a result, the concepts of weak convergence and the finite-dimensionality of the image space of the random operators become irrelevant. Furthermore, the development of nonlinear versions of the Skhorem and the Dudley-Stone theorem has been explored, showing that the coherent laws of an infinite sequence of monotone operators can be determined if the operators themselves are bounded in their ranges.

We've proven that for c being at least 100,000,000 and n being at least 4c-2, any n-vertex graph with a high level of connectivity, and whose vertices can be split into two sets A and B where A contains at least the independence number of B, will inevitably contain all possible cycles with a length of c. Furthermore, the stated condition for A and B, along with the lower bound on the number of vertices, can both be optimal.

We've investigated how different initial conditions of energy density influence the flow patterns and particle production within a two-dimensional, time-dependent simulation. Starting with various forms of energy density - including a uniform distribution and a form based on the energy-momentum tensor from large collision studies - we observed that the shape of the energy density has a significant impact on the final results. This is particularly evident in the interaction between the medium and the flowing particles, revealing that these systems tend to decelerate and even reverse direction. To address this issue, we've developed an analytical method to determine the equilibrium state the system will eventually reach. Our findings suggest that these non-uniform systems gradually build up a characteristic "ridge" pattern over time, which is consistent with the equilibrium state that these systems would theoretically start with. This ridge pattern is formed by the gradual transport of energy away from the center, and our observations provide valuable insights into the complex behavior of the systems being studied.

A nonlinear relationship between observations and predictions in many scientific problems makes the prediction task difficult. While physics-informed neural networks have been effective in discovering governing laws and making predictions for linear cases, they are not always suitable for handling highly nonlinear systems. This work introduces SASK, a new approach that utilizes an iterative process to linearize complex systems and enables making predictions. The SASK method incorporates these linearized components into a neural network, which is then optimized by using a loss function based on available data and physics-based principles. This can be thought of as a neural operator that is learned and can be trained efficiently by utilizing previously learned models, thus reducing training time. This is demonstrated through the solution of the Navier-Stokes equations, where reducing the training time for subsequent models resulted in a significant decrease in time from hours to minutes. Furthermore, incorporating the linearized components into these complex systems enables making accurate predictions for systems with small variations in boundary values, thus bypassing the need for retraining the model and significantly reducing training time. This efficiency is shown by successfully predicting the Navier-Stokes equations with different boundary values and by accurately solving a more complex system, specifically a free surface Navier-Stokes model.

We investigate the resonance structure of the hydrogen molecular ion affected by a DC electric field and microwave radiation by solving the Schrödinger equation using the Floquet-Borkis method. Considering three coordinate systems, such as prolate spheroidal, oblate spheroidal and parabolic coordinates, we derive and compare the resonance parameters of the water molecule under a DC field and microwave field with established literature and theoretical values. Notably, our calculated parameters align with previous studies but differ slightly in magnitude, while the resonance parameters match those obtained from time-dependent Schrödinger equation studies.

We investigate how the Sinkhorn algorithm responds to the Schrödinger problem when no solution exists, utilizing insights from large deviation theory. We demonstrate in a mathematical proof that the algorithm converges towards a point, the location of which is defined by the problem's constraints if a solution exists. Conversely, if the problem has no solution, the algorithm converges towards a point that corresponds to a quadratic minimization over the set of possible outcomes constrained by the problem's constraints. The case in which the constraints form a subspace is also examined in detail.

Measurements of the cross-section for top-quark pair production in proton-proton interactions at a 7 TeV center-of-mass energy have been carried out using a detector based on collisions recorded during the first period of the Large Hadron Collider. The cross-section values were determined using different datasets with integrated luminosities of 0.92 and 0.72 inverse femtobarns, alongside corrections for detector impacts. The findings agree with theoretical models of Quantum ChromoDynamics to within approximately 10 percent but exhibit variability between experimental datasets that corresponds to a 1.8 standard deviation discrepancy.

We investigate the time-evolution of entanglement in a disordered, interacting spin system that can be measured at specific locations by coupling to a central qubit or cavity mode. By utilizing a feasible experimental setup and analyzing various observation methods, our study reveals how this class of quantum systems develops long-lasting entanglement in the spins and intense light-matter interactions. Specifically, we demonstrate how modifying system-size and coupling strength to the cavity can enhance interaction rates and improve overall performance.

In this study, specific subordination principles are introduced along with established conditions for generalized Bessel functions to exhibit particular characteristics of convexity and starlikeness within the unit disk. The findings are demonstrated through mathematical proof.

The pandemic's profound and lasting impact on our daily interactions cannot be overstated. As the health emergency subsided, the profound changes it brought to our social fabric are now more apparent than ever. With the death toll reaching over six million, the pandemic's severe consequences on urban diversity have left an indelible mark. This article will explore how the pandemic affected my work as a social designer through a series of reflections on three projects spanning five years, from March 2020 to May 2021. These reflections will delve into the pandemic's diverse consequences on digitalization, the erosion of community resilience, and emerging opportunities for social innovation. This ultimate goal will be to foster the restoration of local networks, intergenerational connections, and face-to-face interactions essential for building enduring resilience.
